Unlike some earlier sheets, almost the entire sheet is concentrated on one major syllabus block—Paging and page tables—and that block appears prominently in both exam documents. In the more recent Gedächtnisprotokoll, Paging/Memory Management was even described as a comparatively extensive exam problem, involving construction of page tables, logical/physical addresses, unit conversions, and an inverted-page-table question. Paging and address translation

That matches the organization of the summary very closely: the summary’s section “7. Paging und Seitentabellen” starts with pages, frames, address decomposition and page tables, and then covers TLBs, effective access time, direct/inverted tables and multilevel page tables. ibn-zusammenfassung ibn-zusammenfassung ibn-zusammenfassung

Why Aufgabe 2 and Aufgabe 6 stand out
Aufgabe 2 is almost exactly the skill tested in the recent exam protocol. The protocol says that the Paging problem required students to create/fill page tables and determine logical and physical addresses, with PIDs and addresses given. Gedächtnisprotokoll_Klausur_ IB… That is essentially what Aufgabe 2 trains.
The 2016 exam is equally direct. It gives a logical address translated to a physical address, asks for its offset, page index and frame number, and then asks for the corresponding entries of both a normal and an inverted page table. ibn-klausur-2016
So for exam preparation I would treat Aufgabe 2 as mandatory.
Aufgabe 6 is even more striking. The 2016 exam asks for the memory requirement of a normal page table and then for the memory requirement of an inverted page table. ibn-klausur-2016 Moreover, the old 2012 minitest included in the same PDF asks:

maximum memory requirement of a page table without hierarchical tables;
what fraction of physical memory an inverted page table would require. ibn-klausur-2016

That is essentially Übung 5, Aufgabe 6, just with the parameters packaged slightly differently. So this is not merely “the same topic”; it is a historically demonstrated exam question form.


Aufgabe 1: important concept, less important packaging
The point of Aufgabe 1 is to make you understand the structural relationship
\[
\text{page number}\longrightarrow \boxed{\text{page table}}\longrightarrow\text{frame number}.
\]
That is exactly the formulation used in the summary: the page number is the index, and the corresponding page-table entry contains the frame number. ibn-zusammenfassung
The student-residence analogy itself is unlikely to appear verbatim on an exam. But once you strip away the analogy, it tests two important questions:

What does a direct page table actually represent?
Why can a direct page table contain an enormous number of unused entries?

So I would understand it thoroughly but not spend much time rehearsing the dormitory analogy itself.


Aufgabe 3: TLB capacity + locality
This one is more sophisticated. You have a 4 KiB page, 4-byte integers, an array accessed with stride (M), and a TLB containing 64 entries. You have to reason about when successive array accesses hit different pages and when the working set exceeds the TLB capacity. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
The summary explicitly treats the TLB as a cache of page-table entries, including TLB hits/misses and the fact that only a small number of pages tend to be accessed frequently. ibn-zusammenfassung
So the knowledge is definitely syllabus material, but the exact “choose (M) and (N)” formulation looks more like a deeper exercise than a historically observed exam problem. I’d therefore study the reasoning, but not prioritize it above Aufgaben 2 and 6.


Aufgabe 4: TLB and context switches
This question tests an important consequence of the fact that different processes have different page tables.
The summary explicitly says that each process needs its own direct page table because different processes may use the same logical addresses while referring to different data. ibn-zusammenfassung
Therefore stale entries such as
\[
p \rightarrow f_A
\]
from process A cannot normally simply remain valid when process B, which may map the same page (p) to (f_B), starts executing.
The “does this also apply to threads?” part is particularly useful because it checks whether you understand that threads of one process normally share the same address space.
This is a good short conceptual-exam-question style, even though neither of our two exam documents directly asks it.


Aufgabe 5: useful, but supplementary
This is the easiest one to deprioritize. It literally asks you to use the Address Translation Simulator and submit a screenshot. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
The translation process it illustrates is important. The activity itself is not.
For exam preparation I’d classify it:

Supplementary visualization exercise — do once if the mechanism is unclear; otherwise skip during final revision.



Aufgabe 7: very useful calculation pattern
This task combines two things:
\[
\text{expected access time}
\]
and
\[
\text{locality / why TLB hit rates are high}.
\]
The summary explicitly contains an expected-access-time calculation for a TLB:
\[
E[X]=h(1+T)+(1-h)(2+T)
\]
for the simple one-level case, together with the interpretation of TLB hit and miss costs. ibn-zusammenfassung
Aufgabe 7 generalizes essentially the same reasoning to a (k)-level page table. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
That makes it quite valuable: it is not merely memorizing a formula—you need to reconstruct the formula from the number of memory accesses.
I would therefore consider it strong exam preparation, even though our two exam samples do not show this exact question.


Aufgabe 8: multilevel tables
This is the sheet’s most comprehensive page-table-structure problem. You have to divide a 32-bit logical address among:

page offset,
level-1 index,
level-2 index,
level-3 index,

and then determine the number of table entries and total maximum memory usage. ueb05-ibn-SS2025
The summary explicitly expects understanding of this structure: upper levels contain addresses of lower-level page tables, while only the lowest level plays the role of the ordinary direct page table. ibn-zusammenfassung
So this is core syllabus material. Its only downside from an exam-preparation perspective is that the exercise is rather extensive. An actual exam might split it into smaller subquestions.



My exam-preparation grouping
If we use the same practical categories we were using for the previous sheets, I would group them approximately like this:

And one especially useful conclusion from this sheet is that “Paging und Seitentabellen” should be treated as a major exam block rather than a peripheral chapter. The 2016 exam allocated 12/52 points to Speicherverwaltung, with almost the entire problem centered on page tables. ibn-klausur-2016 The newer memory protocol again reports a large Paging/Memory-Management problem involving page tables, address translation, size calculations, and inverted page tables. 3. Counting processes
Every process that reaches a successful fork() creates one additional process.
Thus, if there are (k) processes immediately before a fork() and all (k) execute it successfully, there will be
\[
2k
\]
processes afterwards.
For \(n\) successive unconditional calls,
fork();
fork();
fork();
the total number is
\[
2^n.
\]
Here, three calls produce \(2^3=8\) processes, including the original process.
This shortcut works only when every existing process executes every call. With conditions, loops, exit(), or exec(), you must trace the individual execution paths.

title: 3  Processes and fork()
text:
4. The safe process-tree method
For each fork():

Identify every process that reaches the call.
Give each of them one new child.
Copy the parent’s current variable values into the child.
Assign the appropriate return value:

parent receives a positive PID;
child receives zero.

Continue tracing every resulting process separately.

Do not count the number of occurrences of the word fork and immediately use \(2^n\). A conditional call may be reached by only part of the process tree.

Example
pid_t p = fork();

if (p == 0)
    fork();
After the first call:

parent: p > 0;
child: p == 0.

Only the child enters the if and executes the second call. Consequently, there are three processes, not four.

title: 3  Processes and fork()
text:
5. Process hierarchy
Each child has:

its own PID;
the PID of its parent, called its PPID.

This produces a process tree. A child created later by an existing child becomes a grandchild of the original process.
The parent and child normally execute concurrently. The scheduler may run either one first, so the order of their output is generally not predictable.
However, the order of instructions inside one process remains fixed.

title: 3  Processes and fork()
text:
6. The five basic process states
The five-state model required by the course is: 01-ibn-zusammenfassung.pdf







State
Meaning




New
The process is being created.


Ready
It can execute but is waiting for a CPU.


Running
Its instructions are currently being executed by a CPU.


Waiting / Blocked
It cannot continue until some event occurs, such as completion of I/O.


Terminated
It has finished execution or has been terminated.



The important distinction is:

Ready: capable of running, but no CPU currently assigned;
Waiting: not capable of continuing yet, even if a CPU were available.


State transitions



Transition
Typical cause




New → Ready
The process is admitted into the ready queue


Ready → Running
The scheduler dispatches it


Running → Ready
Time slice expires or the process is preempted


Running → Waiting
It requests I/O or waits for an event


Waiting → Ready
I/O completes or the awaited event occurs


Running → Terminated
It finishes or calls exit()



Normally, a process does not move directly from Waiting to Running. Once its event occurs, it becomes Ready and waits to be selected by the scheduler.


Where does fork() fit?
A parent must be Running to execute fork(). The operating system creates a child, which passes through New and becomes Ready. The scheduler then decides whether the parent or the child runs next.
Calling fork() does not guarantee that the child executes first.

title: 3  Processes and fork()
text:
7. Common exam traps

Counting only the children and forgetting the original parent.
Assuming that only the child continues after fork().
Reversing the return values: the child gets 0; the parent gets the child’s PID.
Assuming the parent always runs before the child.
Forgetting that descendants inherit the current value of previously assigned variables.
Using (2^n) even though some calls are conditional.
Confusing Ready with Waiting.
Claiming that I/O completion causes Waiting → Running directly.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Race conditions
A race condition exists when the correctness or result of a program unintentionally depends on the timing or execution order of concurrent operations.
A typical race condition requires:

shared state;
concurrent accesses to that state;
at least one access that modifies it;
insufficient synchronization.

The output may differ between executions because the scheduler can produce different interleavings.

Critical region
A critical region or critical section is a part of a program that accesses shared data and must not be executed simultaneously with a conflicting critical region.
entry protocol

critical region

exit protocol

non-critical region
The entry and exit protocols are implemented using a mutex, semaphore or another synchronization primitive.


Requirements of a good mutual-exclusion solution
A correct solution should provide:

Mutual exclusion: conflicting threads are never simultaneously inside their critical regions.
Progress: a thread outside its critical region must not unnecessarily prevent others from entering.
No timing assumptions: correctness must not depend on CPU speed or the number of cores.
No starvation/bounded waiting: a thread requesting entry should not be postponed forever.

The first is a safety property: “nothing bad happens.” Progress and absence of starvation are liveness properties: “something good eventually happens.”

text:
Atomicity
An operation is atomic if other threads cannot observe or interrupt a partially completed execution of that operation.
For example, the abstract operation
wait(S)
must itself be atomic. If two threads could simultaneously test and decrement the semaphore non-atomically, the semaphore would not provide synchronization.
Protecting a critical region does not mean that all its ordinary instructions become individually atomic. It means that the entry protocol ensures that only the permitted thread or threads can execute that region.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Semaphores
A semaphore contains:

a nonnegative count representing available permits or resource instances;
an associated queue of blocked threads;
two atomic operations, conventionally called wait and signal.

Other common names are:



Operation
Alternative names




wait(S)
P(S), down(S), sem_wait(S)


signal(S)
V(S), up(S), post(S), sem_post(S)




wait(S)
Conceptually:
if a permit is available:
    consume one permit
    continue
else:
    block until a permit becomes available
Thus, wait may block.


signal(S)
Conceptually:
make one permit available
if a thread is waiting:
    wake one waiting thread
signal does not normally block.
The implementation may represent blocked threads using negative values or separate queues, but exam solutions should normally describe the abstract behaviour rather than depend on a particular representation.


Binary and counting semaphores
A binary semaphore has at most one available permit:
Semaphore mutex = 1
A counting semaphore can represent several identical resource instances:
Semaphore printers = 3
Up to three successful wait(printers) operations can occur before another thread must release a permit.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Mutual exclusion with a semaphore
Initialize the semaphore to 1:
Semaphore mutex = 1
Every thread uses:
wait(mutex)

    // critical region

signal(mutex)
The first thread consumes the only permit. Other threads calling wait(mutex) must block until the first thread calls signal(mutex).
The protected operation must lie entirely between wait and signal:
wait(mutex)
counter = counter + 1
signal(mutex)
Protecting only the load or only the store would still allow an unsafe interleaving.

Mutex versus binary semaphore
At the level required by many introductory exercises, a mutex can be viewed as a binary lock. More precisely:

a mutex normally has an owner;
only the thread that locked it should unlock it;
a semaphore represents permits and does not necessarily have ownership.

Semaphores can consequently express both mutual exclusion and dependencies between different threads.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Enforcing an execution order
Suppose block X in Thread 1 may execute only after block Y in Thread 2.
Initialize a semaphore to zero:
Semaphore finished_Y = 0
Thread 1:
wait(finished_Y)
X
Thread 2:
Y
signal(finished_Y)
Why initialize it to zero?

If Thread 1 reaches wait first, it blocks.
After Thread 2 completes Y, signal provides the permit.
If Thread 2 finishes first, the semaphore retains the permit. Thread 1’s later wait consumes it and continues immediately.

This is what is meant by saying that a semaphore has memory: an earlier signal can be remembered in its counter.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Blocking versus busy waiting
A primitive can wait in two ways.

Busy waiting
while lock is unavailable:
    repeatedly test lock
The thread remains runnable and consumes CPU time. A lock implemented this way is often called a spinlock.
Busy waiting can be reasonable for extremely short waits inside kernels or multiprocessor code, but it is inefficient for long waits.


Blocking
If the resource is unavailable:

the thread is placed in a waiting queue;
its state becomes Waiting/Blocked;
another runnable thread receives the CPU;
a later signal makes the blocked thread Ready.

Notice that waking a thread normally produces:
Waiting → Ready
not immediately Waiting → Running.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Condition variables
A condition variable allows a thread to sleep until some condition involving shared state may have become true.
It must be used together with:

a predicate, such as count > 0 or production_done;
a mutex protecting that predicate;
the condition variable on which threads wait.

Canonical pattern:
lock(mutex)

while (!condition) {
    cond_wait(condition_variable, mutex)
}

// condition is true; access shared state

unlock(mutex)
cond_wait(cv, mutex) performs three important actions:

atomically releases mutex and puts the caller to sleep;
waits for a notification;
reacquires mutex before returning.

The atomic release-and-sleep step prevents the following lost-wakeup race:

waiter checks that the condition is false;
notifier makes it true and sends a signal;
waiter goes to sleep after the signal;
no future signal arrives.


Why while, not if?
After waking, the thread must check the predicate again because:

wakeups may be spurious;
another awakened thread may acquire the mutex first and consume the resource;
a notification means “the condition may now be true,” not “the condition is guaranteed to remain true.”

Correct:
while (count == 0)
    cond_wait(not_empty, mutex)
Unsafe:
if (count == 0)
    cond_wait(not_empty, mutex)


signal versus broadcast

cond_signal(cv) wakes at least one waiting thread.
cond_broadcast(cv) wakes all threads waiting on cv.

A producer adding one item normally needs to wake only one consumer. If production_done becomes true and every consumer must notice it and terminate, a broadcast is appropriate.
The awakened threads do not all enter the critical region simultaneously: each must first reacquire the mutex.


Condition variables do not remember notifications
If cond_signal or cond_broadcast is called while nobody is waiting, the notification disappears.
This differs from a semaphore:
signal(S)
with no waiter increments or preserves the semaphore’s permit count, so a later wait(S) can consume it.
A mutex remembers whether it is currently locked, but an unlock is not a stored notification that a future thread can consume.


Why update and signal under the mutex?
The standard protocol is:
lock(mutex)
done = true
cond_broadcast(done_changed)
unlock(mutex)
The mutex makes changing the predicate and notifying waiters part of one synchronized protocol. A waiter cannot slip between checking done and beginning to wait. When it wakes and reacquires the mutex, it sees a consistent value of done.


Example: producer-consumer queue

producers create items / jobs and insert them into a shared queue.
consumers remove items
a consumer cannot remove an item while the queue is empty
instead of repeatedly checking the queue in a busy loop, it sleeps on not_empty


Concrete Example: downloading and playing a video
The producer downloads video chunks:
network -> buffer
The consume decodes and siplays them
buffer -> video player

the downloader puts some chunks into the buffer
the player begins consuming them
both continue concurrently

Other canonical examples:

a network interface receives packets, while an application processes them
a web server accepts requests while worker threads handle earlier requests
one thread reads files, while another processes their contents.
keyboard input arriving while the application processe earlier input

The general pattern is that

a buffer crates a pipleline and absorbs temporary differences in speed between producers and consumers



Benefits of concurrent production and consumption

lower latency: the consumer can start as soon as the first item exists instead of waiting for all items
higher throughput: production and consumption may overlap

one core produces while another consumes
a network or disk operation runs while the cpu processes previous data

bounded memory use: for a large or infinite stream, we may use a bounded buffer:
producer -> fixed-size buffer -> consumer
A bounded buffer typically uses two predicates and two condition variables:
std::condition_variable not_empty; // consumers wait here
std::condition_variable not_full; // producers wait here




Complete producer-consumer program
shared Queue jobs
shared Mutex mutex
shared ConditionVariable not_empty
shared Boolean production_done = false

function producer():
    for number from 1 to 10:
        job = create_job(number)

        lock(mutex) //begin critical region 1

        jobs.push(job)
        signal(not_empty)

        unlock(mutex)

        // end critical region 1

    // no more jobs will be produced
    lock(mutex) // begin critical region 2

    production_done = true
    broadcast(not_empty)

    unlock(mutex) // end cr 2

function consumer(worker_id):
    while true:
        lock(mutex)

        while jobs.empty() and not production_done:
            wait(not_empty, mutex)
        
        if jobs.empty() and production_done:
            unlock(mutex)
            return
        
        job = jobs.pop()

        unlock(mutex)

        // processing is done outside of critical region
        process(job)

function main():
    producer_thread = start_thread(producer)
    consumer_thread_1 = start_thread(consumer, 1)
    consumer_thread_2 = start_thread(consumer, 2)

    join(producer_thread)
    join(consumer_thread_1)
    join(consumer_thread_2)

    print("all jobs completed")


Bounded-buffer producer-consumer problem
uses a shared queue with a fixed maximum capacity

consumers wait on not_empty when the buffer is empty
producers wait on not_full when the buffer is full
a mutex protexts the buffer and related shared state

The bounded buffer provides backpressure: if consumers cannot keep up, producers are forced to wait instead of allowing the queue to grow indefiniely.

Practical Example
Consider a program that reads large imagems from disk and processes them:

the producer reads images and places them in memory
several consumers resize / transform or analyze the images
each image may occupy considerable memory

An unbounded queue could consumer all abailable memory if disk reading is temporarily faster than image processing. A buffer limited to, say, five images ensures that at most five unprocessed images are held in memory


Complete typed pseudocode

// shared state

constant BUFFER_CAPACITY = 5
constant NUMBER_OF_JOBS = 20
constant NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS = 2

shared Queue<Job> jobs

shared Mutex mutex
shared ConditionVarialbe not_empty
shared ConditionVarialbe not_full

shared production_done = false


// producer
function producer() -> Void:
    for job_number from 1 to NUMBER_OF_JOBS:
        job = new Job(job_number)

        lock(mutex)

        while jobs.size() == BUFFER_CAPACITY:
            wait(not_full, mutex)
        
        // buffer is not full
        jobs.push(job)

        // buffer is not empty
        signal(not_empty)
        
        unlock(mutex)

    lock(mutex)

    production_done = true
    // every sleeping consumer must discover that production is finished
    broadcast(not_empty)

    unlock(mutex)

// consumer

function consumer() -> Void:
    while true:
        lock(mutex)

        while jobs.empty() and not production_done:
            wait(not_empty, mutex)
        
        // no buffered jobs remain, and no new jobs will arrive
        if jobs.empty() and production_done:
            unlock(mutex)
            return

        // buffer not empty
        job = jobs.pop()

        // at least one producer may now be able to proceed
        signal(not_full)

        unlock(mutex)

        process(job)


// main program

function main() -> Void:
    consumers = new Array<Thread>(NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS)

    for i from 0 to NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS - 1:
        consumers[i] = start_thread(consumer)

    producer_thread = start_thread(producer)

    join(producer_thread)
    
    for i in [1, NUMBER_OF_CONSUMERS]:
        join(consumers[i])

    print("all jobs completed")






join()



join() does not end the thread. It makes the calling thread wait until another thread has finished.
consumer_thread_1 = start_thread(consume, 1)

... 

join(consumer_thread_1)

start a new htread executing consumer(1)
continue executing the main thread
When join(consumer_thread_1) is reached, pause the main thread until consumer_thread_1 terminates

This guarantees that the main thread will not prematurely terminate before consumer_thread_1 does, which would be possible because the scheduler can decide to execute the return or the final statement of main, ending the main thread, before consumer_thread_1 is finished

Producer–consumer pattern
For a bounded buffer of capacity (N), a semaphore solution uses:
Semaphore empty = N
Semaphore full  = 0
Semaphore mutex = 1
Producer:
produce(item)

wait(empty)
wait(mutex)
insert(item)
signal(mutex)
signal(full)
Consumer:
wait(full)
wait(mutex)
item = remove()
signal(mutex)
signal(empty)

consume(item)
Interpretation:

empty counts free slots;
full counts stored items;
mutex protects the buffer data structure.

Do not acquire mutex before waiting for empty or full. Otherwise a thread might sleep while holding the buffer lock, preventing the other side from changing the condition it is waiting for.

title: 4  Race conditions, semaphores and synchronization
text:
Simplified read–write lock
The reader-writer problem arises whenever many threads access the same shared data, where:

readers only inspect the data and may safely run concurrently
writers modify the data nad therefore need exclusive access


Example 4.1 (In-memory cache) A web server may maintain a shared cache

readers: look up cached pages or database results
writers:

insert new entries
remove expoired entries
refresh existing entries




Naive Solution
Suppose:
Semaphore S = N
A reader consumes one permit:
lock_read:
    wait(S)

unlock_read:
    signal(S)
A writer attempts to consume all (N) permits:
lock_write:
    repeat N times:
        wait(S)

unlock_write:
    repeat N times:
        signal(S)
This appears to permit either:

up to (N) simultaneous readers; or
one writer holding every permit.

But lock_write is not atomic.
For (N=3), two writers could execute:
W1: wait(S)   // S: 3 → 2
W2: wait(S)   // S: 2 → 1
W1: wait(S)   // S: 1 → 0
W2: wait(S)   // blocks
W1: wait(S)   // blocks
Neither writer can acquire all three permits, and neither can release its partial acquisition because it has not entered the critical region. This is a deadlock.
A simple repair serializes writers while they collect the permits:
Semaphore S = N
Semaphore writer_gate = 1

lock_write:
    wait(writer_gate)
    repeat N times:
        wait(S)
    signal(writer_gate)

unlock_write:
    repeat N times:
        signal(S)
Only one writer may now attempt the multi-step acquisition.
This repair prevents the writer–writer split deadlock, but it does not necessarily guarantee fairness: continuously arriving readers might still starve a writer.
One correction to retain from your earlier work: your old Sheet 3 answer identified the interleaved writer acquisition, but described it as permitting simultaneous writing. The direct consequence is instead the deadlock shown above. 14-Operating-Systems-and-Networs-SoSe-25-Solutions.pdf


Solving fairness Problem

First approach: sared entrance gate
Semaphore S = N
Semaphore entry_gate = 1

// reader
lock_read:
    wait(entry_gate)
    wait(S)
    signal(entry_gate)

unlock_read:
    signal(S)


// writer
lock_write:
    wait(entry_gate)
    repeat N times:
        wait(S)

unlock_write:
    repeat N times:
        signal(S)
    signal(entry_gate)
Here, once a writer acquires entry_gate

no new reader can beign acquiring a permit
existing readers may finish and release their permits
the writer eventually collects all N permits
the writer holds both the entrance gate and all permits during its critical region

But the fairness is still not guaranteed, if the semaphore is completely unfair. It is still possible for newly arriving readers repaetedly to acquire the gate before hte writer:
reader 1 releases gate
reader 2 immediately acquires it
reader 2 releases gate
reader 3 immediately acquires it
The the writer could still starve. But with a fair / FIFO semaphore
waiting order
    writer -> reader 2 -> reader 3
new readers cannot overtake the writer.






Note



A fair / FIFO alone would solve the starvation problem but the writer could still wait very long, because its wait requests in the loop could be often intersparsed with the requests of readers continiously arriving

Treating counter++ as an indivisible operation.
Thinking a race requires multiple CPU cores.

Assuming condition-variable notifications are remembered.

title: 5  Paging fundamentals
text:
1. What paging does
The central skill for today is:
virtual address → page number and offset → frame number → physical address.
The other main skill is determining what a page table has one entry for, then multiplying its number of entries by the stated entry size.
A process uses logical/virtual addresses (logische/virtuelle Adressen). A physical address (physische Adresse) identifies a location in physical memory. The MMU (Memory Management Unit) translates addresses using mappings established by the operating system.
Paging divides:
A page and a frame have the same size. A resident virtual page occupies one physical frame. Consecutive virtual pages can occupy nonconsecutive frames.
For example, virtual pages 0, 1 and 2 could occupy frames 7, 2 and 11. The program still accesses a continuous sequence of virtual addresses; translation accounts for the physical arrangement.
Virtual addresses are process-specific. Page 1 of process A and page 1 of process B need not contain the same data or map to the same frame. In the normal-table model, each process has its own table. Threads sharing one address space share its mappings.

title: 5  Paging fundamentals
text:
a process’s virtual address space into fixed-size pages (Seiten);
physical memory into equally sized frames (Seitenrahmen).





Fragmentation
External fragmentation means free memory is split into separate holes, preventing an allocation that requires a sufficiently large contiguous region. Basic paging avoids this problem for frame allocation: a process’s pages can use scattered free frames.
Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. Paging can waste space in a partially used page, for example at the end of a page-aligned buffer.
For a page-aligned region of \(L\) bytes and page size \(P\):
\[
N=\left\lceil\frac{L}{P}\right\rceil,
\qquad
\text{allocated bytes}=NP,
\qquad
\text{unused bytes}=NP-L.
\]
Example: 5,000 bytes with 4 KiB pages require two pages, allocating 8,192 bytes and leaving 3,192 bytes unused.
Use the ceiling, not ordinary rounding or rounding down. This calculation counts the region’s data pages, excluding page-table storage.

\boxed{p=\left\lfloor\frac{V}{P}\right\rfloor,\qquad d=V\bmod P.}
\]
The offset satisfies:
\[
0\le d<P.
\]
Because \(P=2^n\), the offset occupies the lowest \(n\) bits. The page number occupies the remaining \(v-n\) bits.



Address
Upper bits

The reasoning is straightforward: \(n\) bits distinguish \(2^n\) byte positions inside one page.
For a full \(v\)-bit virtual address space:
\[
\text{virtual bytes}=2^v,
\qquad
\boxed{\text{virtual pages}=2^{v-n}.}
\]
For \(R\) bytes of physical RAM, assumed here to consist of complete, consecutively numbered frames:
\[
\boxed{F=\frac{R}{P}.}
\]
Representing \(F\) frame numbers requires:
\[
\left\lceil\log_2F\right\rceil\text{ bits}.
\]
If \(R=2^r\) bytes, this is \(r-n\) bits.
A physical address width does not necessarily mean all those addresses have RAM installed. Use the stated RAM capacity when counting physical frames.

Short worked example
Take:

24-bit virtual addresses;
2 KiB pages;

Then:
\[
P=2^{11}\text{ bytes}
\]
means 11 offset bits.
The virtual page number has:
\[
24-11=13\text{ bits},
\]
giving \(2^{13}\) possible virtual pages.
The RAM contains:
\[
\frac{2^{23}}{2^{11}}=2^{12}
\]
frames, requiring 12 bits per frame number.
For \(V=6,197\):
\[
6197=3\cdot2048+53,
\]
so:
\[
p=3,\qquad d=53.
\]

title: 5  Paging fundamentals
text:
3. Normal page tables and translation
A normal/direct, single-level page table (normale/direkte, einstufige Seitentabelle) is indexed by the virtual page number.
In the simplified mapping-only model:
\[
\operatorname{PT}_{\mathrm{PID}}[p]=f.
\]
The index is the page number; the entry contains the frame number.
The page number need not be stored again in the entry because its position already identifies it.
A complete page-table entry, or PTE, can also contain:







Field
Purpose




Frame number
Identifies the resident page’s physical frame


Present/resident indicator
Indicates whether a resident mapping is available


Access permissions
Indicate whether a read, write or execution is allowed



Whether the virtual page belongs to an allocated region must also be known. The encoding of allocation and residency varies; use the exercise’s stated model.
To translate a permitted access to a resident page:

Split \(V\) into \(p\) and \(d\).
Select the current process’s table and obtain \(f\) from entry \(p\).
Form the physical address:

\[
\boxed{A=fP+d.}
\]
The offset is unchanged. Paging moves an entire page to a frame while preserving each byte’s position inside it.
Continuing the example, if \(\operatorname{PT}[3]=9\):
\[
A=9\cdot2048+53=18,485.
\]
Frame 9 is a number; its base address is \(9P\). These are different quantities.
Frame 0 is a valid frame, not automatically an indication that a page is absent.

When translation cannot complete

If a page belongs to the address space but is not resident, the access faults; the OS may bring the page into RAM and retry the instruction.
If the address is not allocated, or the access violates its permissions, the access is invalid. The OS handles the fault, normally reporting an error or terminating the process.

Do not calculate a successful physical access from an absent or disallowed entry. The detailed handling and page-replacement policies belong to later topics.


Reconstructing entries from address pairs
If a successful mapping \(V\rightarrow A\) is given, calculate:
\[
p=\left\lfloor V/P\right\rfloor,
\qquad
d=V\bmod P,
\qquad
f=\left\lfloor A/P\right\rfloor.
\]
First check:
\[
\boxed{V\bmod P=A\bmod P.}
\]
Different offsets make the pair impossible under ordinary paging with that page size.
For a fixed mapping snapshot, two observations from the same process and same virtual page must also produce the same frame. A mapping can change over time, so the snapshot assumption matters.
Once the checks pass, enter \(p\rightarrow f\) in that process’s table.
Multiple observations from one page establish one entry, not one entry per observation. Unmentioned pages cannot be classified as unmapped merely because they do not appear in a partial trace.

title: 5  Paging fundamentals
text:
4. Inverted page tables
An inverted page table (invertierte Seitentabelle) has one entry per physical frame, usually in one system-wide table.
In the basic model with one recorded mapping per occupied frame:
\[
\operatorname{IPT}[f]=(\mathrm{PID},p).
\]
The frame number is the index, so it need not also be stored in the entry. The entry stores the process identifier and virtual page number, plus any specified flags.
The PID is necessary because different processes can use identical virtual page numbers.








Property
Normal table
Basic inverted table




One entry for each
Virtual page
Physical frame


Index
Page number \(p\)
Frame number \(f\)


Mapping information stored
Frame number \(f\)
PID and page number \(p\)


Organization
One table per process/address space
One system-wide table


Translation lookup
Index the process’s table with \(p\)
Find \((\mathrm{PID},p)\); its row index gives \(f\)



For PID 6 with page 3 in frame 9:
\[
\operatorname{PT}_6[3]=9,
\qquad
\operatorname{IPT}[9]=(6,3).
\]
An inverted table is not directly indexed by the virtual page number. Conceptually, translation searches for \((\mathrm{PID},p)\). Practical implementations can accelerate this search; those mechanisms are outside today’s scope.
Once \(f\) is found:
\[
A=fP+d
\]
still applies.

Shared memory: the important limitation
Normal tables express shared memory directly:
\[
\operatorname{PT}_A[2]=11,
\qquad
\operatorname{PT}_B[5]=11.
\]
Both virtual pages map to frame 11. With equal offsets, they refer to the same physical byte.
A basic inverted entry containing only one \((\mathrm{PID},p)\) pair cannot represent both mappings in row 11. Supporting this requires additional mapping information, for example a list of aliases or a separate structure.
Shared memory is problematic for this simple representation; it is not fundamentally impossible with inverted tables.

title: 5  Paging fundamentals
text:
5. Calculating page-table memory
Always separate:
\[
\boxed{
\text{table bytes}
=
\text{number of entries}
\times
\text{bytes per entry}.
}
\]

Normal table
For a full, flat table covering every page in a \(v\)-bit virtual address space, with page size \(2^n\) and \(E_N\) bytes per entry:
\[
\boxed{T_N=2^{v-n}E_N\text{ bytes per process}.}
\]
The entry count depends on the virtual address space, not RAM capacity or the number of resident pages.
Unmapped pages still have slots in this full-table model.
With \(k\) processes, each having its own such table:
\[
T_{N,\mathrm{total}}=kT_N.
\]


Inverted table
With \(R\) bytes of RAM, page size \(P\) and \(E_I\) bytes per inverted entry:
\[
\boxed{T_I=\frac{R}{P}E_I\text{ bytes system-wide}.}
\]
Its fraction of RAM is:
\[
\boxed{\frac{T_I}{R}=\frac{E_I}{P}.}
\]
Multiply by 100 to express this as a percentage.
This fraction is independent of RAM capacity when page size and entry size remain fixed. Do not multiply a single global inverted table’s size by the number of processes.
These formulas count the stated entries and exclude auxiliary search structures. Normal and inverted entries need not have the same size.


Worked comparison
Assume:

28-bit virtual addresses;
4 KiB pages;
64 MiB RAM;
4-byte normal entries;
8-byte inverted entries.

The normal table requires:
\[
T_N=2^{28-12}\cdot4
=2^{18}\text{ bytes}
=256\text{ KiB per process}.
\]
The inverted table requires:
\[
T_I=\frac{2^{26}}{2^{12}}\cdot8
=2^{17}\text{ bytes}
=128\text{ KiB total}.
\]
Its fraction of RAM is:
\[
\frac{8}{4096}=\frac1{512},
\]
or approximately:
\[
0.1953\%.
\]


Address-field width is not complete entry size
If there are \(2^{14}\) frames, a frame number needs 14 bits.
That does not mean a complete normal PTE occupies 14 bytes, or even exactly 14 bits. Flags, storage alignment and the stipulated format also matter.
If a question specifies a 4-byte entry, use 4 bytes. If it does not, state your assumed entry size or leave the answer in terms of \(E_N\). This assumption is needed for Sheet 5 A6(1).
For a tightly packed \(B\)-bit inverted entry containing a \((v-n)\)-bit page number and \(s\) flag bits, the remaining PID capacity is:
\[
b_{\mathrm{PID}}=B-(v-n)-s,
\]
giving:
\[
2^{b_{\mathrm{PID}}}\text{ possible PID values}.
\]
This assumes no other fields and no reserved PID values. It bounds how many process identifiers the format can distinguish; the actual simultaneous process count also depends on other resources.
The frame number and offset need not be stored: the row identifies the frame, and the input address supplies the offset.

title: 5  Paging fundamentals
text:
Common exam traps

Confusing page size with offset width: 4 KiB means 12 offset bits.
Changing the offset during translation: valid address pairs have the same remainder modulo \(P\).
Mixing numbers and addresses: the physical address is \(fP+d\), not \(f+d\).
Ignoring the PID: the same virtual address can translate differently in different processes.
Swapping indices and contents: normal \(p\rightarrow f\); inverted \(f\rightarrow(\mathrm{PID},p)\). Frame 0 is valid.
Confusing entries, bits and bytes: multiply the entry count by the complete entry size in bytes.
Counting the wrong address space: normal tables count virtual pages; inverted tables count physical frames.
Mixing binary and decimal units or rounding allocations down: state KB conventions and use a ceiling for required pages.

title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
1. Hierarchical page tables
Day 3 established how a virtual page number maps to a physical frame. Today adds three mechanisms:
The strongest direct Day 4 evidence in the 2016 exam is the question about approximating last-access times using hardware reference bits. Multilevel tables, TLB calculations, and replacement traces are supported primarily by the assignments and the explicit study plan. The 2026 memory protocol confirms paging’s importance but does not explicitly report these advanced mechanisms.
Throughout this unit, memory is byte-addressable, page sizes are powers of two, and KiB/MiB use binary units.

title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
Why divide a page table into levels?
A full flat page table contains one entry for every possible virtual page, including unused virtual regions.
For example, 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KiB pages give:
\[
2^{32-12}=2^{20}
\]
entries. At four bytes per entry, that is 4 MiB per process, even if the process uses little memory.
A hierarchical table divides this mapping into smaller tables. The root contains references to tables at the next level; only the final level contains mappings to data frames.
Its main space advantage is:

Tables for unused virtual-address regions need not be allocated.

Hierarchy does not make a fully populated table smaller. When every possible mapping is represented, the leaf entries still exist, and the upper levels add overhead.


Address decomposition and translation
With \(v\)-bit virtual addresses, page size \(2^n\) bytes, and \(k\) table levels:
\[
\boxed{v=b_1+b_2+\cdots+b_k+n}
\]
Here, \(b_i\) is the number of bits indexing level \(i\); the final \(n\) bits are the offset.
For three levels:



Virtual-address field
Function




\(i_1\): \(b_1\) bits
Select an entry in the root table


\(i_2\): \(b_2\) bits
Select an entry in the chosen level-2 table


\(i_3\): \(b_3\) bits
Select an entry in the chosen leaf table


\(d\): \(n\) bits
Select a byte within the mapped data frame



The translation proceeds as follows:

The current process’s page-table root address identifies the root.
Root entry \(i_1\) identifies the physical base address of a level-2 table.
Entry \(i_2\) of that table identifies a leaf table.
Leaf entry \(i_3\) contains the data-frame number \(f\), together with flags.
Form the physical address:

\[
A=f\,2^n+d.
\]
The offset remains unchanged. The table levels collectively translate the virtual page number.
If entries occupy \(E_i\) bytes, the selected entry at level \(i\) is located at:
\[
\text{table base}+i_iE_i.
\]
Intermediate entries identify next-level tables; leaf entries identify data frames. Confusing those contents is a common mistake.


Counting tables and entries
An index with \(b_i\) bits selects among \(2^{b_i}\) entries in one table at that level.
For a fully populated three-level hierarchy:









Level
Number of tables
Entries per table
Total entries at that level




1
\(1\)
\(2^{b_1}\)
\(2^{b_1}\)


2
\(2^{b_1}\)
\(2^{b_2}\)
\(2^{b_1+b_2}\)


3
\(2^{b_1+b_2}\)
\(2^{b_3}\)

Thus, with \(E\) bytes per entry at every level:
\[
\boxed{
T_{\max}
=
E\left(
2^{b_1}
+
2^{b_1+b_2}
+
2^{b_1+b_2+b_3}
\right)
}
\]
More generally:
\[
T_{\max}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}E_i\,2^{b_1+\cdots+b_i}.
\]
This counts page-table storage only, excluding the process’s data pages.


Short worked example
Suppose a system has:

24-bit virtual addresses;
256-byte pages;
two levels, each using eight index bits;
four-byte entries.

The address split is:
\[
\underbrace{i_1}_{8}
\mid
\underbrace{i_2}_{8}
\mid
\underbrace{d}_{8}.
\]
Each table has 256 entries and occupies:
\[
256\cdot4=1\text{ KiB}.
\]
The maximum hierarchy contains one root and 256 leaf tables:
\[
T_{\max}=257\text{ KiB}.
\]
If the process uses pages in only two root-index regions, it needs one root and two leaf tables:
\[
T_{\text{allocated}}=3\text{ KiB}.
\]
This assumes complete tables are allocated and ignores allocator overhead. Even if only one entry in a leaf table is used, the whole leaf table occupies 1 KiB.
Do not assume a table occupies exactly one page. That is a common design choice, but follows only when the specified entry count and entry size make it true.

title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
2. The TLB: caching translations
A Translation Lookaside Buffer, or TLB, is a small, fast hardware cache of page translations.
Conceptually, an entry contains:
\[
(\text{address-space identity},\text{virtual page})
\longrightarrow
(\text{physical frame},\text{permissions}).
\]
It caches a translation, rather than the page’s data.

Hit and miss
For a permitted access:







Event
What happens




TLB hit
Obtain the frame number from the TLB; access the data at \(fP+d\)


TLB miss, page resident
Walk the page table, obtain the mapping, refill the TLB, and complete the access


TLB miss, page nonresident
The page-table lookup detects absence; a page fault transfers control to the OS



A TLB miss therefore does not imply a page fault.
A page-table walk may be performed by hardware or by software, depending on the architecture. For these exercises, the essential point is the extra translation work on a miss.


Why a small TLB helps
Programs exhibit:

Temporal locality: recently accessed pages are often accessed again.
Spatial locality: nearby addresses often lie within the same page.

For example, a page-aligned array of four-byte integers contains 1,024 integers per 4 KiB page. Sequentially reading those integers reuses one translation many times.
The TLB’s nominal coverage, sometimes called its reach, is:
\[
\text{TLB entries}\times\text{page size}.
\]
A 64-entry TLB with 4 KiB pages can cache translations covering 256 KiB.
Coverage alone does not determine the miss rate. Access order, alignment, associativity, and replacement policy also matter. For a simplified fully associative LRU TLB, repeatedly cycling through more distinct pages than it can hold can produce a miss on every access.


Quantitative access time
The course explicitly includes this calculation.
Assume:

\(k\) page-table levels;
one RAM access per level on a miss;
all pages and page tables are resident;
no additional caches or overlapping accesses;
TLB lookup time \(t_{\mathrm{TLB}}\);
RAM access time \(t_{\mathrm{RAM}}\);
TLB hit ratio \(h\);
every access first performs a TLB lookup.

Then:
\[
t_{\text{hit}}=t_{\mathrm{TLB}}+t_{\mathrm{RAM}},
\]
\[
t_{\text{miss}}=t_{\mathrm{TLB}}+(k+1)t_{\mathrm{RAM}}.
\]
The \(+1\) is the actual data access after the \(k\) table accesses.
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{EAT}
=
h\,t_{\text{hit}}+(1-h)t_{\text{miss}}
=
t_{\mathrm{TLB}}+\left[1+k(1-h)\right]t_{\mathrm{RAM}}
}
\]
For two levels, \(t_{\mathrm{TLB}}=5\) ns, \(t_{\mathrm{RAM}}=80\) ns, and \(h=0.95\):
\[
\operatorname{EAT}
=
5+[1+2(0.05)]80
=
93\text{ ns}.
\]
Without a TLB, the simplified two-level translation plus data access costs \(3\cdot80=240\) ns.
Convention note: the supplied solutions omit TLB lookup time from the miss branch. That requires a different timing assumption or an approximation. State your model; with the sequential lookup model above, it belongs in both branches.
These formulas exclude page faults. Fetching a missing page can be much more expensive than a resident-page access.


Process and thread switches
The same virtual page number can map to different frames in different processes.
Without address-space tags, cached translations must be invalidated when switching address spaces. Otherwise, process B could use process A’s translation.
With address-space identifiers, translations from multiple address spaces can coexist safely if correctly tagged.
Switching between threads that share one address space does not by itself require a TLB flush.

title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
3. Demand paging and page-fault handling
Paging provides address translation. Demand paging additionally allows a valid virtual page to be absent from RAM until needed.
A nonresident page may have contents in an executable file, another mapped file, or swap storage. A newly allocated page may instead be initialized with zeros. A page fault therefore does not always require reading an existing page from disk.
For today’s replacement exercises, a page fault means that the referenced page is absent from the available frames.

The basic sequence
When an access references a valid but nonresident page:

The hardware detects the missing resident mapping and raises a page fault.
The OS checks whether the access is valid and permitted.
The OS obtains a frame:

use a free frame if one is available;
otherwise select a resident victim page.

If necessary, preserve the victim’s modified contents.
Load or initialize the requested page.
Update page-table entries and invalidate stale cached translations.
Restart the faulting instruction.

An invalid address or forbidden operation cannot be repaired simply by loading a page.


Page fault versus replacement
A page fault requires replacement only when no suitable free frame is available.
Consequently:

Loading the first page into initially empty memory causes a page fault.
It does not evict another page.
Once all allocated frames are occupied, a fault requires a victim under the exercise’s fixed-frame model.

There are also two distinct kinds of eviction:



Eviction
What is removed?




TLB-entry eviction
A cached translation


Page replacement
A resident page’s contents from its frame



Removing a TLB entry leaves the page resident.


Reference and dirty bits
Hardware maintains flags associated with pages:








Bit
Meaning
Set by




R / accessed bit
The page has been referenced since the bit was cleared
Hardware on access


M / dirty bit
The page has been modified since its contents were made clean
Hardware on write



Reads and writes both count as references. A read alone does not make a page dirty.
The OS clears bits when appropriate. A dirty victim generally needs its modified contents preserved before its frame is reused. A clean page with an unchanged backing copy can usually be discarded without write-back.

title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
4. FIFO, LRU, and Clock
All three policies select among resident pages when replacement is necessary.

FIFO: oldest arrival
First In, First Out replaces the page that entered memory earliest.
Maintain a queue from oldest to newest:

Hit: leave the queue unchanged.
Fault with free space: load the page and append it.
Fault with full memory: remove the oldest page and append the new page.

A frequently accessed page can still be FIFO’s victim because hits do not renew its arrival time.


LRU: oldest last access
Least Recently Used replaces the page whose most recent access occurred furthest in the past.
For manual simulation, maintain an order from least to most recently used:

Hit: move the referenced page to the most-recent end.
Fault: load the page as most recently used.
If memory is full, first remove the least-recent page.

Exact LRU needs recency information updated on every reference. Maintaining that precisely can be expensive; hardware bits support cheaper approximations.


One state illustrating the difference
Suppose three frames receive:
\[
A,\ B,\ C,\ A.
\]
All three pages are resident.

FIFO order: \(A,B,C\). Its next victim is A.
LRU order: \(B,C,A\). Its next victim is B.

FIFO asks “Who arrived first?” LRU asks “Who was used least recently?”


Clock / Second Chance
Clock implements a second-chance policy using:

frames arranged in a circular order;
one reference bit per resident page;
a hand pointing to the next candidate.

Use this explicit convention:

Every completed reference sets the page’s \(R=1\), including the reference that loads it.
Hits do not move the hand.
On replacement:

if the candidate has \(R=0\), replace it;
if it has \(R=1\), clear the bit and advance;
repeat until a victim is found.

Load the new page with \(R=1\), then advance the hand to the next frame.

Queue-based Second Chance applies the same idea by moving an oldest page with \(R=1\) to the back after clearing its bit. Clock represents that rotation with a circular hand.
Initialization conventions can change a trace. Some teaching examples initialize newly loaded pages differently. Always follow the stated convention.


Why Clock differs from exact LRU
After \(A,B,C,A\), suppose all bits are 1 and the hand points to A.
On a fault for D, Clock:

Clears A’s bit.
Clears B’s bit.
Clears C’s bit.
Returns to A, now with \(R=0\), and replaces it.

Exact LRU would replace B.
Clock knows that all three pages were referenced since their bits were cleared. It does not know the exact ordering of those references.


Reliable manual tracing
For each reference:

Check whether the page is already resident.
Mark hit or fault.
On a fault, fill a free frame or select a victim.
Update the policy’s metadata.
Record the complete state after the reference.

Keep physical frame positions fixed in your table. Record FIFO/LRU order separately; changing recency order does not move page contents between frames.



Policy
Metadata you must update




FIFO
Arrival queue; unchanged on hits


LRU
Recency order; updated on every reference


Clock
R bits and hand position



FIFO can exhibit Belady’s anomaly: adding frames can increase faults for some reference strings. Exact LRU does not have this anomaly. Neither FIFO nor LRU wins on every individual reference string.

text:
5. Approximating recency with R bits
An R bit answers:

Has this page been referenced at least once since the bit was last cleared?

It does not record:

how many references occurred;
their exact times;
their ordering relative to references to other pages.


Periodic sampling
Divide time into epochs. At each epoch boundary, the OS conceptually performs:
for each page-table entry being monitored:
    if entry.R == 1:
        entry.last_observed_epoch = current_epoch

    entry.R = 0
During the next epoch, hardware sets the bit again if the page is accessed.
A page with an older last_observed_epoch has not been observed in use for longer and is a plausible victim.
However, two pages accessed in the same epoch receive the same approximate timestamp, even if one was accessed at its beginning and the other immediately before the scan.
This is LRU-like approximation, not exact LRU.
Real implementations must ensure that clearing the bit makes subsequent accesses observable despite cached translations. For exam purposes, assume the required synchronization and invalidation are included in the stated operation cost.


Sampling versus Clock
Both use hardware reference bits, but differently:



Mechanism
When are bits inspected and cleared?




Periodic epoch sampling
At regular time intervals


Basic Clock
While searching for a victim



Clock’s hand position and previous scans influence its information. Its bits do not necessarily describe one common sampling interval.


R-bit scanning overhead
The Sheet 6 A4 model scans full flat page tables.
Let:

\(m\): number of processes;
\(v\): virtual-address width;
\(2^n\): page size;
\(c\): cycles to sample and clear one entry;
\(f_{\mathrm{CPU}}\): CPU cycles per second.

Then:
\[
N_{\text{scan}}=m\,2^{v-n},
\]
\[
C_{\text{scan}}=c\,m\,2^{v-n},
\]
\[
\boxed{
t_{\text{scan}}
=
\frac{c\,m\,2^{v-n}}{f_{\mathrm{CPU}}}
}
\]
This counts entries in the stipulated tables. It does not require every virtual page to be resident or even allocated.
For the original sheet’s parameters:
\[
t_{\text{scan}}
=
\frac{10\cdot20\cdot2^{20}}{10^9}
\approx0.2097\text{ s}.
\]
If scans start every \(T\) seconds, including scanning time within that interval, their CPU-time fraction is:
\[
\boxed{\alpha=\frac{t_{\text{scan}}}{T}}.
\]
To stay at or below a budget \(\alpha_{\max}\):
\[
\boxed{T\ge\frac{t_{\text{scan}}}{\alpha_{\max}}}.
\]
For a 10% budget, the original parameters require at least about 2.10 seconds, rather than exactly 2 seconds.
The tradeoff is:

Short epochs: finer recency information, more scanning overhead.
Long epochs: less overhead, more references grouped into indistinguishable intervals.

There is no universally correct epoch length. Derive it from the stated budget and explain the loss of precision.

title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
Common exam traps

Counting one table instead of a whole level: distinguish entries per table, tables per level, and total entries per level.
Claiming hierarchy always saves memory: sparse allocation saves memory; a fully populated hierarchy adds upper-level overhead.
Confusing intermediate pointers with data-frame numbers.
Equating a TLB miss with a page fault, or a page fault with an eviction.
Forgetting the final data access in TLB timing calculations.
Updating FIFO on hits, or failing to update LRU on hits.
Tracing Clock without specifying the hand and R-bit conventions.
Treating R bits as exact timestamps: they record occurrence within an interval, not access order.
Scanning physical frames when the problem specifies full per-process flat tables, or mixing CPU cycles with seconds.

Exercise 1 — A sparse three-level address space
A machine uses:

30-bit virtual byte addresses;
1 KiB pages;
three page-table levels with index widths 6, 7, and 7 bits, from root to leaf;
four-byte entries at every level.

Entry 9 of that table contains leaf-table base 0xA000.
Leaf entry 17 maps to frame 73 and permits the access.

the virtual byte address;
the physical address of each of the three selected entries;
the resulting physical data address.

the number of tables at each level;
the total entries at each level;
the total page-table memory.

The process additionally allocates page \((0,3,3)\). Does this require another page-table allocation? What about allocating \((0,4,0)\)? Explain.

Give the total initial TLB misses, page faults, and data-page evictions.

t_{\mathrm{TLB}}=8\text{ ns},\qquad
t_{\mathrm{RAM}}=70\text{ ns},\qquad
h=0.90.
\]

A separate workload repeatedly reads one byte from pages:

\[

All four pages remain resident. Its initially empty TLB is fully associative, holds three translations, and uses exact LRU. Determine the hit/miss behavior and explain whether it implies page faults.


C. Address-space identity

Process Q maps its page 0 to frame 12. Explain what could go wrong if an untagged TLB retains P’s page-0 translation when switching to Q.
Does switching between two threads of P create the same problem? Explain.





Exercise 3 — Complete FIFO, LRU, and Clock traces
A process has three initially empty frames, numbered 0, 1, and 2. All referenced pages are valid. The reference string is:
\[
A,\ B,\ C,\ A,\ D,\ B,\ E,\ A,\ B,\ C,\ D,\ E.

A. FIFO and exact LRU

Simulate FIFO and exact LRU separately.
After every reference, record:

all three frame contents;
hit or fault;
victim, if any;
FIFO queue or LRU order.

Count page faults and evictions for each policy.
Identify the first reference at which their victim choices differ. Explain using their metadata.



B. Clock
Use these conventions:

The hand initially points to frame 0.
Empty frames are filled at the hand, then the hand advances.
Every loaded or referenced page has \(R=1\).
Hits leave the hand unchanged.
During replacement, clear and pass over candidates with \(R=1\).
Replace the first candidate with \(R=0\), set the new page’s bit to 1, and advance the hand.


Simulate Clock for the same complete string.
After each reference, record:

frame contents and R bits;
the hand position;
hit/fault and victim.

At the first replacement, list every frame inspected, including repeated inspections. Compare Clock’s victim with exact LRU’s.

Exercise 4 — R-bit evidence and its cost

A. What can sampling reveal?
Four resident pages A, B, C, and D initially have:
\[
R=0,\qquad\text{last observed epoch}=0.
\]
At the end of each epoch, the OS updates the approximate timestamp of every page with \(R=1\), then clears all R bits.
The references are:



Epoch

B. Scanning overhead
A different system has:

32-bit virtual addresses;

a 2 GHz CPU;

No reduction under the specified model. It scans every entry of every full flat table, regardless of residency.

Supplementary Matrial
I agree with your suggestion to keep the detailed implementation relatively low priority for now. However, after checking the uploaded materials, epoch-based LRU approximation is actually more exam-relevant than you suspected.
The IBN summary explicitly describes storing the last 8, 16, or 32 observations of each page’s R bit. Moreover, the 2016 exam (Aufgabe 2.5, 4 points) asks how hardware R bits can be used to approximate the last access time. Übungsblatt 6, Aufgabe 4 asks about scanning overhead and choosing an epoch length. 
ibn-zusammenfassung.pdf
ibn-klausur-2016.pdf
Our previous assignment-sheet analysis also classified these calculations as high priority. So I wouldn’t interpret the omission as a deliberate decision that the mechanism is unimportant. A concise explanation should have been included.

1. How epochs and shifting registers work
An epoch (Epoche) is simply a fixed time interval, for example 100 ms.
For each relevant page, the OS maintains:

The hardware-maintained R bit.
A software-maintained history register, say 8 bits long.

At the end of each epoch, the OS performs three operations:

Read the current R bit.
Shift the history register one position to the right, inserting R as the leftmost bit.
Clear R for the next epoch.

In pseudocode:
for each resident page p:
    history[p] = (history[p] >> 1) | (R[p] << 7)
    R[p] = 0
Here history[p] is an 8-bit value, and >> and << are bit shifts.

Concrete example
Suppose page A is accessed during epochs 1 and 3, but not during epochs 2 and 4.

The leftmost bit represents the most recent epoch; older observations move to the right.
Compare two pages:






Figure 6.1: epoch bits



The aging algorithm treats these bit histories as unsigned integers and preferentially evicts the page with the smallest value.
In this case, B is selected.
This approximates LRU because an older reference contributes a smaller value than a recent one. It is not exact LRU: the history also reflects how many epochs contained references, and accesses within an epoch cannot be ordered.



2. Where is the history stored?
Normally, the history register is maintained by the operating system in software, not by the MMU in a dedicated hardware field.
It is useful to distinguish:








Information

The history could be stored in an auxiliary array indexed by virtual page, or in metadata associated with resident physical pages.
Some architectures offer software-available PTE bits, but a conventional hardware-defined PTE does not provide a dedicated 8-, 16-, or 32-bit aging register.
One interesting correction to the IBN summary: it suggests an inverted page table is necessary to examine the pages of all processes. That is not generally required. The OS can scan conventional page tables belonging to different processes or maintain separate metadata structures. In fact, Übungsblatt 6, Aufgabe 4 explicitly assumes direct page tables, one per process.

3. How important is this for the exam?
I would distinguish the following levels of preparation.







Knowledge
Priority




Explain that the CPU sets R on access

High

Medium


Know kernel data structures and exact implementation details
Low



The trade-off for epoch length is also worth remembering:

Short epochs: Better time resolution, but more frequent scanning and therefore higher overhead.
Long epochs: Lower scanning overhead, but less precise information about recent accesses.


My recommendation
Spend enough time to understand the shifting-history mechanism and be able to explain it in 3–4 sentences. You now have sufficient background for that.
Then continue with the main Day 4 material. The detailed implementation of aging counters, page metadata, and reverse mappings can wait until after the core preparation plan.
One especially useful connection: The 2016 exam’s question about approximating last-access time can be answered directly with the R-bit sampling and history mechanism above. So this is one of those small details worth retaining, even under time pressure.
